title: Why Language Models Hallucinate
summary: Theory paper (OpenAI and Georgia Tech). Part 1 reduces generation to binary classification ('Is-It-Valid'): a base model's generative error rate is lower-bounded by roughly twice its misclassification rate on deciding whether an output is valid, minus calibration terms, so cross-entropy pretraining produces errors even with error-free data. For 'arbitrary facts' with no learnable pattern, the hallucination rate after pretraining is lower-bounded by the singleton rate (fraction of facts seen exactly once), recovering Kalai and Vempala (2024). Part 2 argues that hallucinations persist after post-training because benchmarks use binary grading, under which abstaining is never optimal (Observation 1); a meta-evaluation of popular benchmarks finds most give no credit for IDK. The proposed fix is socio-technical: put explicit confidence targets (answer only if confidence > t; wrong answers cost t/(1-t)) into mainstream evaluations, which makes 'behavioral calibration' auditable.
setting: Theory (computational learning theory reduction, Good-Turing singleton argument), illustrative prompts to DeepSeek-V3, ChatGPT, Llama-4, Claude 3.7 Sonnet; meta-analysis of ~10 popular benchmarks' grading schemes. No training experiments.

quotes.quote: However, we show that even if the training data were error-free, the objectives optimized during language model training would lead to errors being generated.
recovers their bound that the hallucination rate, after pretraining, should be at least the fraction of training facts that appear once.
However, we claim that further reduction of hallucinations is an uphill battle, since existing benchmarks and leaderboards reinforce certain types of hallucination.

finding that the vast majority of popular evaluations have binary grading. Therefore, additional hallucination evaluations may not suffice when the primary evaluations penalize honestly reporting confidence and uncertainty.

Let us refer to this as behavioral calibration–rather than requiring the model to output a probabilistic confidence (Lin et al., 2022a), it must formulate the most useful response in which it is at least confident.
Our formalism does not distinguish between errors of different magnitudes or degrees of uncertainty. Clearly, the correct/incorrect/IDK categories are also incomplete.
In pretraining, we show that generative errors parallel misclassifications in supervised learning, which are not mysterious, and naturally arise due to the minimization of cross-entropy loss.

key_numbers.quote: For instance, if 20% of birthday facts appear exactly once in the pretraining data, then one expects base models to hallucinate on at least 20% of birthday facts.
language models are optimized to be good test-takers, and guessing when uncertain improves test performance.

limitations_stated: The formalism considers only plausible strings, does not distinguish errors of different magnitude, treats correct/incorrect/IDK as an incomplete trichotomy, does not model pragmatics of hedging, and does not address ambiguity-driven errors. Search/RAG does not escape Observation 1. No empirical training study.
open_questions: Whether changing mainstream benchmark scoring to explicit confidence targets actually changes post-training outcomes (no experiment). How to train behavioral calibration directly and audit it across thresholds. How the singleton-rate bound interacts with RL fine-tuning rather than pretraining.
sense_of_alignment: Uses 'aligned' for evaluations and models whose incentives reward calibrated uncertainty: 'most evaluations are not aligned', benchmarks 'that are misaligned but dominate leaderboards', and 'Model A is an aligned model that correctly signals uncertainty and never hallucinates'. The sense is incentive alignment between scoring rules and honest reporting, not a model's goals.
